competition: All-Russian Astronomy Olympiad — final stage, grade 11

problems.problem:
1. Echo of a cosmic explosion

A powerful short gamma-ray pulse from a distant supernova was recorded simultaneously on 12 April by artificial satellites of the Earth and of Mars, and also by the space station "Ulysses", which at that moment was located above the north pole of the Sun. In which constellation was the supernova, if Mars was at opposition to the Sun on that day? Neglect the inclination of the plane of the Sun's equator to the plane of the ecliptic.

2. Orbital radio telescope

The Russian space radio telescope "Radioastron" will be put into an elliptical orbit with an apogee distance of 330 000 km. Together with ground-based radio telescopes it will form a very-long-baseline interferometer. With what best spatial resolution will it be possible to study the region of the active nucleus of a galaxy having a redshift of 0.5? "Radioastron" will operate at wavelengths from 1.35 to 90 cm.

3. Eclipse in space

On the night of 1 to 2 June 2011 there will be a partial solar eclipse. Its maximum phase, visible on the Earth, will be 0.60 and will be seen at $21^\mathrm{h}16^\mathrm{m}$ Universal Time at the bright solar midnight in the north of the territory of Russia. The angular diameters of the Sun and the Moon will then be equal, $31.5'$. Imagine that at the same moment cosmonauts on board an orbital station observe a central total solar eclipse. Above which point of the Earth's surface are they at that time? Determine the coordinates of this point. The orbit of the station is geosynchronous, circular, with a period of one sidereal day; the plane of the orbit is inclined to the plane of the Earth's equator.

4. Mirror-white wanderer

To study the interplanetary medium, a probe of a new generation has been launched into the Solar System. It is spherical, very small, and made of ultralight materials. One of its hemispheres is covered with a perfectly reflecting mirror layer, and the other with a white porous material resembling snow, which also reflects 100% of the incident radiation. The probe was delivered to some point of the Solar System and initially brought to rest relative to the Sun, without rotation. The Sun then illuminated half of each of the probe's hemispheres. With which hemisphere will the probe begin to turn towards the Sun immediately after it starts operating? The materials of which the probe consists are stable, do not evaporate and do not change their properties with time. The centre of mass of the probe is at its geometric centre. Do not take into account the action of the planets and small bodies of the Solar System on the probe.

5. A distant expedition

A space expedition arrived at an inhabited planet in a distant star system. The temperature conditions on this planet were similar to those on the Earth. The escape velocity (second cosmic velocity) for the surface of this planet turned out to be exactly half of the third cosmic velocity and 50 times smaller than the escape velocity for the surface of the star around which the planet orbits. The orbit of the planet is circular. Find the effective temperature of the central star.

6. Multitude of civilizations

Imagine that near every tenth star in our Galaxy there is one inhabited planet. The inhabitants of all these planets search for other civilizations using only data of ultra-precise photometry of stars. The accuracy of brightness measurements is $0.00001^\mathrm{m}$ for stars of $0^\mathrm{m}$ and becomes 2 times worse for stars 4 times fainter, 3 times worse for stars 9 times fainter, and so on. How many civilizations will as a result be able, in the foreseeable future (within the next 100 years), to discover the planet Earth near the star Sun? Take the number density of stars in the disc of the Galaxy to be $1\ \mathrm{pc^{-3}}$.

1. Ground tracks of artificial satellites

You are given two drawings showing the ground tracks of artificial Earth satellites (the trajectories of the point on the Earth's surface where the satellite is seen at the zenith) in an equirectangular projection. The orbits of the satellites are circular. Determine the orbital periods of the satellites and the inclinations of their orbits to the plane of the Earth's equator.

2. Orbital photograph of the Moon

In the photograph, taken from an artificial Earth satellite, you see the full Moon above the edge of the Earth, marked with a red line. Estimate at what height above the Earth's surface the artificial satellite is at the moment the picture was taken. Take the atmospheric refraction at the Earth's surface at the horizon to be $35'$. Assume that at all heights the atmosphere has the same chemical composition and a temperature of $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Do not take into account absorption and scattering of light in the atmosphere, nor the effects of clouds.

3. Extraterrestrial observatory

At a new observatory built on the surface of one of the bodies of the Solar System, high-precision measurements of the apparent positions of celestial objects are made. The graph shows the displacements of a certain star and of a distant quasar next to it relative to their mean positions along some direction on the sky. The displacement of the quasar and the star in the perpendicular direction is small and is not observed. It is known that the star is single and has no proper motion. What is the distance to the star? From which object of the Solar System were the observations made?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/astronomy-olympiads-bank/main/images/ruao-2011-d2-q3-1.png

XI.1. Upper culmination of Vega

At which latitudes on the Earth is it possible (at least once a year) to see the star Vega at upper culmination in a dark sky, with the centre of the Sun more than 6 degrees below the horizon? Take the coordinates of Vega to be $\alpha = 18^\mathrm{h}$, $\delta = +39^\circ$; neglect refraction.

XI.2. Telescope and the Sun

A telescope with an objective of diameter 20 cm is pointed at the Sun. Is it safe to look into it if a diaphragm has been placed in the focal plane of the telescope that covers the whole Sun except a single sunspot 20000 km across? The diameter of the exit pupil of the eyepiece equals the diameter of the pupil of the observer who has decided to look into this telescope. Compare the illuminance produced by the sunspot through this telescope with the illuminance from other celestial objects.

XI.3. Minima of an eclipsing variable

The primary minimum of an eclipsing variable binary star has a depth of $1^\mathrm{m}$. What can the depth of the secondary minimum of this star be? Consider the stars to be spherical; neglect the reflection of light from the surfaces of the stars and the limb darkening of their discs.

XI.4. Aluminium sail

A perfectly reflecting flat aluminium solar sail revolves around the Sun in a circular orbit of radius 1 a.u. with a period of 1.5 years. The sail is always perpendicular to the direction to the Sun. Find the thickness of the sail. The density of aluminium is $2.7\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Do not take into account the interaction of the sail with the planets.

XI.5. Transit of Venus through the centuries

On 4 June 1769 in Saint Petersburg, at a specially built observatory, the Russian Empress Catherine II first observed a transit of Venus across the disc of the Sun and then (on the same day!) a partial solar eclipse. Estimate after how many years it will again be possible on our planet to observe a transit of Venus across the disc of the Sun and a solar eclipse with an interval of less than one day.

XI.6. Accretion onto a neutron star

A neutron star moves at a speed of 100 km/s through a cloud of molecular hydrogen with a temperature of 10 K and a density of $10^3\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. Estimate the rate at which the neutron star will gain mass by accretion. Do not take into account collisions between the particles of the cloud.

XI.1. Mountains and stars

The photograph given to you (author: A.B. Gorshkov) was taken somewhere in the northern hemisphere. Estimate the latitude of the place of observation, the azimuth of the middle of the frame, and the absorption near the horizon. In solving the problem you may use the attached star chart of the same region of the sky.

XI.1. The Sun at stellar midnight

Determine whether there exist points on the Earth with the following property: every time the sidereal time in Oryol is $0^\mathrm{h}$, the Sun is certainly shining at these points of the Earth (unless there are clouds). Determine the coordinates of these points, if they exist. The coordinates of the city of Oryol: $53^\circ$ N, $36^\circ$ E.

XI.2. Escape from the Sun

Suppose the Sun began to lose mass at a rate of 1 billion tonnes per second. How far will the Earth move away from it in 1 year? Take the initial orbit of the Earth to be circular.

XI.3. Conjunction of Venus and Jupiter

The planets Venus and Jupiter come into conjunction with each other, having equal equatorial angular sizes. What is the angular distance between Venus and the Sun at that moment? Consider the orbits of Venus, the Earth and Jupiter to be circular and lying in one plane.

XI.4. A brief encounter

A certain star flew past the Sun at a minimum distance of 1 pc. 100 thousand years later its brightness in the Earth's sky had decreased by $2^\mathrm{m}$. What is the velocity of the star relative to the Sun (in km/s)? Consider the physical properties of the star to be constant in time.

XI.5. Blinking planets

Imagine that the Sun has become a short-period variable star with a period of 125 minutes. With practically the same period the brightness of the planets seen from the Earth began to vary, and for one outer major planet the maxima could be observed at the same time as the maxima of the Sun's brightness. Which planet is it?

XI.6. Meteor track

With a fixed digital camera with a lens of focal length 50 mm and a sensor with a diagonal of 27.3 mm and a format of $3000\times2000$ elements, a long-exposure image of the starry sky was taken. It recorded the passage through the zenith of a meteor of the Perseid stream, which is of cometary origin. The meteor has a length of $20^\circ$, and its image on the picture has, on average, the same width and brightness as the trail of Vega ($\alpha=18.5^\mathrm{h}$, $\delta=+38^\circ$, $0^\mathrm{m}$), which was also in the frame. Estimate the size of the meteoroid if it is known that it flew horizontally, lit up and went out at a height of 100 km. Assume that 1% of the kinetic energy of the meteoroid is converted into visible light. The speed of the meteoroids of the Perseid stream on entering the atmosphere is 59 km/s. Neglect the decrease of speed in the atmosphere.

XI.1. Planet and ring

The graph shows the brightness of Saturn in the Earth's sky as a function of time during the first 30 years of the 21st century (approximately one orbital period of the planet). From this graph, estimate the ratio of the mean geometric albedos (in the direction of the light source) of Saturn and of its ring. The polar radius of Saturn is 0.9 of its equatorial radius; the inner and outer radii of the ring are 92 and 134 thousand km. Consider the ring to be solid and homogeneous.

Before you are portions of the spectra of the Sun and of the star 109 Tauri (spectral class G8), obtained on the same day from the same place at approximately the same altitude above the horizon. The spectral region and the wavelength scale of both spectra coincide; the wavelength increases from left to right. In the spectra of both stars one can see lines belonging to the stars themselves and also telluric lines of water vapour arising in the Earth's atmosphere. The wavelengths of the strongest water-vapour lines in this region (in angstroms) are given in the table. Mark the stellar lines in the spectra and find the radial velocity of the star 109 Tauri relative to the Earth.

XI.3. Bright stars in the dusty disc

The diagram shows the relation between the colour indices U−B and B−V for bright stars from the BSC catalogue (Bright Star Catalog, stars down to $6.5^\mathrm{m}$ in the V band). Determine the distances to the single stars 1, 2 and 3 from this catalogue, located in the disc of the Galaxy, whose data are also shown on the diagram. The interstellar absorption of light in the neighbourhood of the Sun in the disc of the Galaxy is $2^\mathrm{m}$ per 1 kpc in the V band and varies with wavelength as $\lambda^{-1.3}$. The spectral curves of the U, B and V bands are shown on a separate graph.

XI.1. Giant pendulum

At the north pole of a distant spherical planet a giant Foucault pendulum was installed. When observed from the point of suspension of the pendulum, the local Sun was always above the horizon, touching it only once a year. The bob of the pendulum was near the surface of the planet, and the period of oscillation was 10 Earth minutes. Find the mean density of the planet. The inclination of the planet's equator to the plane of its orbit is half that of the Earth. Neglect atmospheric effects and the angular size of the star.

XI.2. The sky of a cluster

In the clear daytime sky of the Earth one can just barely see Venus at its greatest elongation from the Sun. How many stars would be visible in the daytime sky of the Earth if the Sun were inside a globular cluster of radius 10 pc consisting of a million stars like the Sun, distributed uniformly over the volume of the cluster? Consider the brightness of the sky background to be the same in all directions.

XI.3. Dust shell

Around a star of spectral class G2V, at a distance of 0.3 a.u., there is a dust shell of thickness 0.01 a.u. with a particle number density of $0.002\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. Determine the luminosity and the mass of the shell. Consider the dust grains to be perfect black bodies of radius $0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$; neglect wave effects.

XI.4. A cooling dwarf

A white dwarf has a mass equal to the mass of the Sun and a radius equal to the radius of the Earth. Its surface temperature is 10 000 kelvin, and the temperature of its interior is 10 million kelvin. Estimate the time during which this object will look like a white dwarf, i.e. will emit energy in the visible range, before it turns into a black dwarf. For simplicity, assume that the heat capacity of the white-dwarf matter corresponds to the heat capacity of an ideal gas.

XI.5. Two eclipses in a row

What is the minimum distance over the Earth's surface that an observer must travel in order to be able to see two partial solar eclipses separated by an interval of one lunar month? Consider the orbits of the Earth and the Moon to be circular.

XI.6. Aitken's catalogue

When compiling his classical catalogue of double stars, the American astronomer Robert Grant Aitken sought to eliminate optical pairs (stars not physically connected with each other) by imposing the following restriction on the double stars:
$$\lg \rho < 2.8 - 0.2m.$$
Here $\rho$ is the angular separation between the components in arcseconds, and $m$ is the stellar magnitude of the brighter of the stars. Estimate the number of optical double stars with both components brighter than $6^\mathrm{m}$ that could nevertheless have got into Aitken's catalogue. Assume that the 6000 stars brighter than $6^\mathrm{m}$ are distributed over the sky at random, and that the number of stars with apparent brightness greater than $J$ is proportional to $J^{-3/2}$.

XI.1. Horseshoe

The asteroid 2010 SO16 moves around the Sun in an orbit practically coinciding with the orbit of the Earth. The figure (viewed from the north pole of the ecliptic) shows the orbit of the asteroid in a reference frame that rotates around the Sun together with the Earth (in this frame the Sun and the Earth are at rest). The trajectory of the asteroid in this frame resembles a horseshoe. Determine the direction of motion of the asteroid along the "horseshoe" and estimate the time in which the asteroid completes one circuit of the "horseshoe". For convenience the width of the "horseshoe" in the figure has been increased 20 times; both parts of the "horseshoe" are equidistant from the orbit of the Earth.

XI.3. Meteor shower

The graphs show the zenithal hourly rate ($ZHR$) of meteors of the Perseid stream as a function of time over the period of activity of this stream in 2013. This quantity is the number of meteors brighter than $6.5^\mathrm{m}$ that an observer could see in one hour over the whole hemisphere of a moonless sky with the radiant of the stream at the zenith, without atmospheric absorption. The second graph shows in more detail the behaviour of $ZHR$ near the maximum (12 August).

Using the graphs, estimate how many Perseid meteoroids producing meteors brighter than $6.5^\mathrm{m}$ at the zenith entered the Earth's atmosphere in 2013. Take the height of the meteors to be 100 km. Assume that the number of meteors brighter than magnitude $m$ in some region of the sky is $\sqrt{2.512}$ (or 1.6) times greater than the number of meteors brighter than magnitude $(m-1)$ in the same region of the sky over the same time. Neglect atmospheric refraction.

XI.1. Twilight

Determine on what part of the Earth's surface twilight (of any stage) is being observed now. Neglect the angular size of the Sun and refraction. Supplement your solution with a drawing.

XI.2. A star on frosted glass

A refracting telescope with a focal ratio of 1:5 and a straight open-frame tube was pointed at a $0^\mathrm{m}$ star. Then the eyepiece was removed and a frosted glass plate was placed in the focal plane. What stellar magnitude will the image of the star on the plate have if the observer is next to the objective (to the side of it, not blocking the path of the star's rays in the telescope)? Assume that the frosted glass scatters all the light to both sides of itself, uniformly in all directions.

XI.3. Planet and cluster

The orbit of the planet Venus is inclined to the plane of the ecliptic at an angle of $3.4^\circ$; the longitude of the ascending node is $77^\circ$. The globular star cluster M19 in the constellation Ophiuchus has the ecliptic coordinates: longitude $257^\circ$, latitude $-3.5^\circ$, angular diameter $14'$. Can Venus (as observed from the Earth) pass across this cluster? Consider the orbits of the planets to be circular.

XI.4. Interplanetary sailing ship

A spacecraft was put into a circular orbit around the Sun with a radius of 1 a.u. After that a solar sail was deployed on it, permanently facing the Sun and reducing the effective force of its attraction by 4%. In the course of its further motion this sail instantly folded up as soon as the spacecraft reached the aphelion of its current orbit, but unfolded again at each perihelion. How many full revolutions around the Sun will this spacecraft make? What will be its further fate? Neglect the interaction of the spacecraft with all bodies except the Sun and its photons.

XI.5. Pulsar timing

At some moment a radio pulsar has a precisely known period of exactly 1 s. How much time will then be needed to discover that the period of this radio pulsar is increasing at a rate of $10^{-15}$? The observing methods make it possible to determine the arrival time of a pulse with an accuracy of $10^{-3}$ s. Consider the pulsar to be at rest relative to the observer.

XI.6. Cold cloud

An interstellar cloud consists of molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) and dust and has the shape of a sphere with a uniform internal distribution of mass. The brightness of distant stars located behind the centre of the cloud is weakened by $1^\mathrm{m}$. At what radius will this cloud begin to contract under the action of its own gravity, if its temperature is 20 K? The mass ratio of gas to dust in the cloud is constant and equal to 100:1; the black dust grains have a radius of $0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, a density of $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, and attenuate light according to the laws of geometrical optics.
